life: Perennial twining vine from a thickened root
edible_parts: Seeds, thoroughly cooked; young pods in some species.
other_uses: A slender perennial vine of the Sonoran and Chihuahuan uplands, twining through grass and shrubs. One of the few wild beans with a foothold in the United States. Native range: the United States (Arizona, New Mexico, Texas); Mexico — north-eastern Mexico, north-western Mexico.
prep: Treated like any wild bean: shell the dry seeds, soak, discard the soaking water and boil hard. Documentation for this species specifically is thin — the genus is broadly edible once cooked, but that is a genus-level inference, not a record for this plant.
harvest: Dry pods late in the season; they shatter, so collect just as they brown.
soil: Well-drained; most of the wild beans grow on dry rocky slopes and in oak or pine-oak woodland.
risks: Never eat Phaseolus seeds raw or undercooked. They contain phytohaemagglutinin, a lectin that causes violent vomiting and diarrhoea — a few raw beans is enough. Soak, discard the water, and boil hard for at least ten minutes; a slow cooker alone does not reach a safe temperature.
